chapter_theme: Under the heading பொருள், nine verses on what wealth does: it overcomes the unreasonable better than force, makes every affair go well, draws the needy and the praise of all, guards the one who guards it, grows from small daily gains, is untouched by petty theft, and leaves the fallen great their standing; one verse warns against scorning a man for his small beginnings.

196.reading: Those who act without understanding and have no merit are best cut off with wealth, for who will hold out once wealth is given; a gift's thrust is stronger than a spear's.
196.nuance: The counsel sets giving against force as ways of dealing with the unreasonable, and ranks giving higher: the proverb's spear and காணி stand for the two. காணி can name a holding of land or a small fraction of money; either way the gift is the sharper weapon. The verse plays on பொருள் as both wealth and the fitting course (பொருளால் அறுத்தல் பொருளே).

pazhamozhi.literal: the thrust of a காணி is stronger than the thrust of a spear

story.act: no story; the proverb opposes the weapon and the gift as two ways to overcome

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the senseless and unworthy are more surely ended by a payment than by force

197.reading: For those who have wealth nothing is out of reach and their affairs go well as they intend, while for those who have none the same affairs turn to trouble; the rich see clearly even in the sea.
197.nuance: The address to the lord of the shining shore (இலங்குநீர்ச் சேர்ப்ப!) is a frame borrowed from the neytal poems. The proverb's sense is not fixed: it may mean that the rich find their way even in a place as trackless as the sea, or that what is in the deep is plain to them.

pazhamozhi.literal: even within the sea they see well

story.act: no story; the proverb states the reach of those who have means

pazhamozhi.applied_to: wealth makes every undertaking go well, where want turns it to hardship

198.reading: Those who hold wealth that is hard to come by do not go looking for those who have business with them, since no one who dug a tank went off in search of frogs.
198.nuance: The tank draws frogs of itself, so the seekers come to wealth and not wealth to them; the verse states this as a law of nature, without praise or blame. The stork asleep on the buffalo's back in the address (எருமைமேல் நாரை துயில்வதியும் ஊர!) is a marutam frame of ease.

pazhamozhi.literal: no one who dug a tank ever went in pursuit of the frogs

story.act: no story; the tank and its frogs are the instance

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the wealthy need not seek those who need them; the needy come of themselves

199.reading: No one, the compassionate or anyone else, fails to praise those who have wealth, and this is the saying that the goods of the fortunate are taken by two.
199.nuance: The point is that even those with அருள், who should be moved by need and not by wealth, join the praise. The proverb's 'two' most likely answers the verse's two kinds of people (the compassionate and the rest), both of whom take from the rich and so praise them; that reading is ours. The address பொருபடைக் கண்ணாய்! is a frame.

pazhamozhi.literal: the goods of the fortunate are taken by two

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the rich and those who live by them

pazhamozhi.applied_to: praise of the rich is universal because all, good and not, share in their goods

200.reading: The owner guards what he owns, and what he owns in turn guards him, as the thicket is strength to the tiger and the tiger strength to the thicket.
200.nuance: The proverb makes wealth and owner each the other's defence: the tiger keeps men from cutting the thicket and the thicket hides the tiger. அடையின் ('if they join') makes the protection depend on the two staying together. The verse thus treats guarding wealth as a gain, not a burden.

pazhamozhi.proverb: புதற்குப் புலியும் வலியே புலிக்குப் புதலும் வலியாய் விடும்
pazhamozhi.literal: the tiger is a strength to the thicket, and the thicket becomes a strength to the tiger

story.act: no story; the tiger and the thicket are the instance of mutual defence

pazhamozhi.applied_to: guarded wealth protects the one who guards it

201.reading: Though one's income be small, if it is gathered every day it grows very great, as gathered light lights the world and gathered drops make a flood.
201.nuance: Two images carry the claim before the proverb: light gathered (ஒளியீண்டி) and drops gathered (துளியீண்டில்), both repeating the verb ஈண்டு of line 1, so accumulation, not the size of the income, is the whole argument.

pazhamozhi.literal: drops, if they gather, give a flood

story.act: no story; the gathered drops are the instance

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a small income gathered daily becomes great wealth

202.reading: Even if the people of one's own town have let us know someone's small beginnings, he should not be despised, for in the old bustling town the calf grazing in the market may also grow into a bull.
202.nuance: முதல் can be the man's origin or his starting capital; under the heading பொருள் the second is likely, but the verse's argument holds for either. The reason given is time: what is small now grows, so contempt based on knowing someone's past misjudges his future. The address இலங்கிழாய்! is a frame.

pazhamozhi.literal: the old calf that grazes in the market may also become a bull

story.act: no story; the market calf is the instance

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a man of known small beginnings may rise, so he is not to be scorned

203.reading: Even if many field labourers steal, the wealth of the very rich does not suffer, for the sea does not run dry because a jackal licked it.
203.nuance: The verse reports the indifference of great wealth to petty loss without judging the thieving labourers (களமர்). The address pictures a town where the dam is opened to drain the water for reaping the ripe paddy, a frame of abundance.

pazhamozhi.literal: will the sea run dry because a jackal licked it

story.act: no story; the jackal at the sea is the instance

pazhamozhi.applied_to: small thefts do not diminish great wealth

204.reading: Will the great rich whom the land knows cower even when they have become poor and withered; though they lie shrunk and shrivelled, no dog sniffs at a tiger's head.
204.nuance: The verse says the standing of those once known as great outlasts their wealth: the mean (the dog) do not dare to approach even the fallen great (the tiger). வட்குபவோ asks whether they will be abashed and expects no. The counsel sits under பொருள் but is about honour in loss of wealth.

pazhamozhi.literal: a dog does not sniff at a tiger's head

story.act: no story; the tiger and the dog are the instance

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the fallen great are not insulted by the mean, nor do they cower

links.note: Kural 759 calls wealth the sharpest steel for cutting down enemies' pride (செருக்கறுக்கும்); Pazhamozhi 196 says wealth given cuts off (அறுத்தல்) the senseless better than a spear.
links.teaches: The pair shows how the Kural's metaphor works in practice: wealth wounds not by being held but by being handed over, so the sharpest blade is a payment that leaves the opponent nothing to resist.
links.list_adds: its proverb sets the gift and the spear side by side and ranks the gift above force, a contrast the couplet only implies.

links.note: Kural 753 calls wealth an unfailing lamp that cuts darkness wherever one goes; Pazhamozhi 197 says the rich see well even in the sea, while the same affairs bring the poor to grief.
links.teaches: Together the two make wealth a means of sight as well as of power: the Kural's lamp travels to any land, and Pazhamozhi carries it into the sea, the place where sight should fail, and adds the poor man for whom the same road is dark.
links.list_adds: it sets the rich man's ease against the poor man's trouble in the same affairs, a contrast the couplet does not draw.

links.note: Naladiyar 283 says bees do not go to the hill where the kanthal has not flowered, so the poor have no kin; Pazhamozhi 198 says no one who dug a tank sought out the frogs, so the rich need not seek those who need them.
links.teaches: Read together, the two nature images state one law from both sides: people are drawn by what can be had, so the rich are sought without seeking and the poor are left without kin, and Pazhamozhi presents as a comfort what the Naladiyar presents as a grief.
links.list_adds: it states the attraction from the side of the owner, who may wait, where the quatrain states it from the side of the poor man who is abandoned.

links.note: Kural 752 says all honour the rich and all scorn the poor; Pazhamozhi 199 says even the compassionate praise the rich and gives the reason in its proverb, that two take from the fortunate.
links.teaches: The Kural states the fact; Pazhamozhi names whom 'all' includes, even those whose compassion should look to need, and explains the praise by interest, since everyone shares in what the rich hold.
links.list_adds: it divides the Kural's 'all' into the compassionate and the rest and supplies a motive, a reason the couplet does not give.

links.note: Naladiyar 280 counts guarding wealth among its bitter sufferings (காத்தலும் ஆங்கே கடுந்துன்பம்); Pazhamozhi 200 says the wealth one guards guards its owner in return, like the thicket and the tiger. The tension holds on the plain reading of both: the Jain quatrain treats guarding as a cost, the proverb as a mutual defence.
links.teaches: The two books judge the same act of keeping wealth oppositely: for the Naladiyar the guard is one more place of suffering, for Pazhamozhi it is what makes wealth a shelter, so the dispute is whether wealth is a burden on its owner or a defence of him.
links.list_adds: its proverb makes guarding reciprocal, which turns the quatrain's one-way burden into an exchange of protection.

links.note: Kural 478 says a small income brings no ruin if outgo is not wider; Pazhamozhi 201 says a small income gathered daily grows great, like drops into a flood.
links.teaches: The pair gives two answers to the small income: the Kural makes it safe by limiting what goes out, Pazhamozhi makes it great by what accumulates over time, so a narrow channel is both a limit to respect and a source that time can enlarge.
links.list_adds: it adds the daily repetition and a second image of gathered light, turning the couplet's balance of channels into growth by accumulation.

links.note: Kural 667 says not to despise anyone for their form, since the great chariot has its linchpin; Pazhamozhi 202 uses the same words (எள்ளாமை வேண்டும்) of one whose small beginnings are known in town, since the market calf may become a bull.
links.teaches: The two give different grounds for the same rule: the Kural's small linchpin matters now by where it stands, while Pazhamozhi's calf matters later by what it grows into, so contempt can err about function or about time.
links.list_adds: it moves the rule from bodily size to known origin or capital, and grounds it in growth over time rather than in present function.

links.note: Pazhamozhi 201 says small drops gathered make a flood; Pazhamozhi 203 says the licks of a jackal do not dry the sea, so petty thefts do not hurt great wealth.
links.teaches: Side by side, the two verses show that the book's arithmetic of small amounts runs only toward growth: daily drops add up to a flood, but daily thefts are not allowed to add up to loss, because the scale of the whole decides which small things count.

links.note: Kural 1043 says poverty destroys at once one's ancient descent and dignity; Pazhamozhi 204 says the great known to the land, though fallen poor, keep their standing, since no dog sniffs at a tiger's head. The tension depends on reading the couplet's தொல்வரவு as inherited standing, as its marks do.
links.teaches: The two disagree on whether poverty can strip inherited greatness: the Kural says it takes descent and dignity together, while Pazhamozhi holds that renown already known to the land outlasts the wealth that won it.
links.list_adds: its proverb of the dog and the tiger's head adds the onlookers, the mean who do not dare, where the couplet speaks only of what the poor man loses.

links.note: Pazhamozhi 89 says the poverty of the great is better than the wealth of the small, as old ghee never sinks below buttermilk; Pazhamozhi 204 says the fallen great are not insulted by the mean.
links.teaches: Together the two verses build the book's case that greatness is not measured by wealth: 89 ranks the poor great above the rich small in worth, and 204 adds that others still treat them so, since the tiger's head is safe from dogs.

source_issues: Pazhamozhi 203: the proverb's நரிநக்கிற்(று) has a bracketed ending in our text, an editorial restoration of the syllable; it does not change the sense.
